scope.concept: The window has to reach back before the rollout. A fixed start stays put while you investigate; “the last 15 minutes” moves with the clock.
scope.narration: The new release began rolling out at ${incident.rollout_clock} (${incident.rollout_ago}). Start the window a little before then, so you can see the rollout and the traffic just before it.
scope.reasoning: Starting just before the rollout puts the old release's healthy traffic next to the new one's. A fixed start keeps both in view, however long you take.
scope.evidence: The histogram should start a little before the rollout.

demonstration.narration: The rollout began at ${incident.rollout_clock}. I'll start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}, the five-minute mark before it. A fixed start keeps the rollout in view, however long we take.
demonstration.evidence: The window now starts at ${incident.window_start_clock}, before the rollout at ${incident.rollout_clock}. The start is a fixed time, so the first requests on the new release can't slide out of view.

drifts.note: You started searching before setting the time window; this step is about choosing when to look.

isolate.narration: Search for the service that stood out in service.name's Top values, across all of its versions. Then read the HTTP status codes in the results.

demonstration.reasoning:
The service and version filter removes other traffic, but it does not pick out errors.

Reading http.response.status_code in the filtered results shows whether requests succeeded or failed, before we compare versions.
demonstration.evidence:
The filtered ${param.incident.service} results show both HTTP ${param.incident.status} and 200 in http.response.status_code.

We still need to compare those results with service.version before we can say what causes the failures.

Those status codes, not the version number alone, show that the new version is bad. Next, when did the first failure happen?

goal.title: Look at which service the window is about
goal.concept: A field's Top values show which service has most of the window's traffic. Then you don't have to guess which one the report means.
goal.narration: The report doesn't name the failing service. Open the service.name field in the sidebar and read its Top values. Which service do most of the window's requests belong to?
goal.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed service would assume the answer. The Top values show which service the incident window is about.
goal.evidence: The service.name Top values show one service carrying most of the window.

demonstration.narration: The report doesn't name the failing service. I'll check service.name Top values to see which service most of this window's requests belong to.
demonstration.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed service would assume the answer. Top values count every request in the window, so the next filter comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.service}, has most of the window's requests, well ahead of the other services. That is the service to compare versions in.

hints: Let the data show which service the incident window is about, instead of assuming one.
Open the service.name field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).
Open service.name and read its Top values; Show me can open the reference field.

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}; this step is about which service the window is about.
You filtered before reading service.name's Top values, so the filter rests on a guess.

goal.title: Find when the new version first appeared
goal.concept: Sorting oldest first puts the start of a change at the top of the table. Newest first hides it at the bottom.
goal.narration: Sort the results oldest first. Then read down service.version to the first request on the new version, and note its time.
goal.reasoning: The brief asks when the first failure happened. Discover lists the newest requests first, so the first failure is at the far end of the list. Sorting the other way brings it to the top.
goal.evidence: The rows run forward from just before the rollout: the old version first, then the new version's first request.

demonstration.narration: I'll sort @timestamp oldest first, so the table reads forward from just before the rollout.
demonstration.reasoning: Discover lists the newest requests first, which puts the start of a regression at the bottom of a long list. Sorted oldest first, the rows read forward in time from the start of the window.
demonstration.evidence:
The first request on ${truth.finding} came at ${incident.first_clock}, and it failed with HTTP ${param.incident.status}. The rows above it are ${param.incident.good_version}, so this is the regression's first appearance, shortly after the rollout at ${incident.rollout_clock}.

${truth.conclusion}

hints: Discover lists the newest requests first; the first appearance is at the other end.
Open the @timestamp column's header menu and choose Sort Old-New, then read down service.version.

drifts.note: That sorts newest first; the first appearance is at the oldest end.
You sorted by ${action.field}; the first appearance is about time, so sort @timestamp.

goal.title: Look at which versions are serving traffic
goal.concept: A field's Top values list every version running, including ones that aren't part of the change you're investigating.
goal.narration: Open service.version in the field list and read its Top values. Which versions of the service are serving requests?
goal.reasoning: A rolling deployment runs the old and new releases side by side, but other versions can be serving traffic too. Know which are present before comparing them.
goal.evidence: The Top values list every version serving the service's requests.

demonstration.narration: I'll check service.version Top values to see which versions of this service are serving requests.
demonstration.reasoning: A rolling deployment runs the old and new releases side by side, but other versions can be serving traffic too. We need to know which are present before comparing any.
demonstration.evidence: Three versions are serving ${param.incident.service}. ${param.incident.bad_version} and ${param.incident.good_version} are the two newest. ${param.incident.legacy_version} is an older release on a legacy pool that this rollout doesn't touch.

hints: Find out which versions are running before you compare any of them.
Open service.version in the field list and read its Top values.
Open service.version's Top values; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: Keep only the rollout's two versions
goal.concept: ‘is one of’ keeps records whose field matches any of several values. It is one filter for a set of values, like or.
goal.narration: Compare only the two releases in this rollout. Use Add filter on service.version with the operator ‘is one of’. Add the two newest versions, and leave out the legacy pool's older version.
goal.reasoning: The legacy pool isn't part of the rollout. If you leave it in, its requests mix into the comparison between the old and new release.
goal.evidence: The filter pill under the query bar keeps both releases of the rollout and leaves the legacy pool out.

demonstration.narration: I'll keep just the rollout's two releases, with one filter that matches either version.
demonstration.reasoning: The legacy pool isn't part of this rollout, so its requests would only confuse the comparison. ‘is one of’ matches any of several values of one field. So a single filter keeps both releases and leaves the legacy version out.
demonstration.evidence: The new filter pill, the small box under the query bar, reads service.version: is one of ${param.incident.good_version}, ${param.incident.bad_version}. Both releases of the rollout stay, and the legacy pool's ${param.incident.legacy_version} requests are gone from the results.

hints: Compare only the two releases the rollout involves, and leave out the version it didn't touch.
Use Add filter: field service.version, operator ‘is one of’, then add each of the two newest versions. (In KQL, service.version: ("a" or "b") does the same.)
Add the filter service.version is one of ${param.incident.good_version}, ${param.incident.bad_version}; Show me can do it for you.
